title: How Books Got into the Bible
lead: The canon (from Greek kanōn, "measuring rod") is the list of books accepted as Scripture. Jews, Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants agree on most of it, and a few books were debated for centuries.

sections.h: The Hebrew Bible and the extra books
sections.b: The Jewish Bible, the Tanakh, has three parts: the Law (Torah), the Prophets (Nevi'im) and the Writings (Ketuvim). Jesus speaks of what was written "in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms" (Luke 24:44). The Septuagint, the Greek translation used by many early Christians, also contained books such as Tobit, Judith, Sirach, Wisdom, 1–2 Maccabees and additions to Esther and Daniel. The Catholic Church affirmed these "deuterocanonical" books at the Council of Trent (1546); Protestants call them the Apocrypha and, following Jerome's doubts, keep them out of the Old Testament or print them separately; Orthodox churches accept a somewhat larger set; the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is larger still and includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees. The older theory that a rabbinic "Council of Jamnia" (about AD 90) closed the Jewish canon is now widely doubted.

sections.h: Disputed books of the New Testament
sections.b: By about AD 200 the four Gospels, Acts and Paul's letters were accepted almost everywhere. Some books took longer. Around AD 325 Eusebius listed James, Jude, 2 Peter and 2–3 John among the "disputed" books (antilegomena) that most churches nonetheless used; Hebrews and Revelation were debated too. Athanasius's Easter letter of 367 lists the 27 books of today's New Testament. The original Syriac Bible (the Peshitta) left out 2 Peter, 2–3 John, Jude and Revelation.

sections.h: Early Christian writings at the edge of the canon
sections.b: 1 Clement follows the New Testament in Codex Alexandrinus, and the Epistle of Barnabas follows Revelation in Codex Sinaiticus. Corinth still read 1 Clement in church about AD 170 (Eusebius, Church History 4.23.11). The list in the Apostolic Canons names two letters of Clement among the books "of the New Testament," after Jude and before Acts (canon 85), a list Westcott judged "of no value" as evidence and probably of the sixth century, and Reid (1908) wrote that "the Coptic-Arabic Church include with the canonical Scriptures the Apostolic Constitutions and the Clementine Epistles." But Eusebius put Barnabas among the rejected writings (Church History 3.25.4) and did not list 1 Clement at all, Athanasius left both out (Festal Letter 39), and the Stichometry of Nicephorus counts Barnabas among the disputed books and the two letters of Clement among the apocrypha (Westcott). See the topic The Apostolic Fathers.

sections.h: Ignatius: letters never put forward as Scripture
sections.b: Unlike the Shepherd and the Epistle of Barnabas, which Eusebius lists among the rejected writings (Church History 3.25.4), Ignatius's letters are not in his lists at all: he presents them among the works of those who 'transmitted the apostolic doctrine to us in writings' (3.37.4-3.38.1), that is, as the letters of a church leader. Ignatius himself disclaims an apostle's authority: 'I do not command you as though I were someone' (Ignatius to the Ephesians 3:1). He calls himself 'the last' of his church, counted worthy only 'from the grace of God' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:1), and sets himself below Peter and Paul: 'They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3). Polycarp collected and sent the letters to Philippi (Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2).

sections.h: A writing no early list names: the Epistle to Diognetus
sections.b: Lake: 'early tradition does not mention the epistle'. It was never weighed for the canon because no one in the early church is known to have read it; it came to light in a single medieval manuscript that seems to have credited it to Justin Martyr (Lake). It is in no church's Bible; the Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it (2240) as a witness to how Christians live as citizens. Its separate ending (11:6) lists 'the Law', 'the Prophets', 'the Gospels' and 'the tradition of the apostles' in one breath.
